title: Edgecase batching + serialization scrapbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a freeform weekly/scrapbook-style note capturing the weird edge cases we hit with batching + serialization under elevated backpressure. Not a finished doc — meant to be a quick notebook for the team to riff on root cause analysis and next actions.

When:
- Observed during spike traffic test on 2027-01-10 23:10 PST (softer production shadow run).
- Corroborated on staging on 2027-01-11 02:40 UTC.

Attendees / who touched this:
- Priya (owner of notes)
- Ethan (kernel patches and instrumentation)
- Lina (KV cache + prefetch configs)
- Rahul (load generator + metrics)

High-level symptom:
- Intermittent 10-30% p95 latency regression for small interactive requests (<=32 tokens) when host is under ~70% GPU util and request QPS has bursty spikes (>800 rps).
- Root-visible anomaly: increased scheduling stalls inside the kernel serialization path and occasional thread contention on the batching queue head.

Initial observations / traces:
- CPU stack samples (10ms) show ~40% of samples in ServeKernel::serialize_batch() on affected hosts.
- Flame graphs point to memory copy and FlatBuffers (schema marshaling) as hotspots.
- KV lookups preceding the serialization are often returning hits but sometimes require on-the-fly decompression (zstd) which amplifies CPU use.

Experiment log (what we tried):
1) Swap FlatBuffers -> newline-delimited JSON during staging run (quick patch):
   - PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve-runtime/pull/1428
   - Result: p95 down ~8% but p50 unchanged. CPU on host moved from 55% -> 63% (serialization moved work from kernel glue into user allocs). Improved scheduling but costlier memory churn.

2) Disable zstd-decompression for KV values when value_age < 30s (temporary guard):
   - Result: removes ~12% of CPU spikes but increased bandwidth usage and memory footprint. Nets: p95 improved slightly during bursts.

3) Batching queue backpressure tweak (lower max_batch_wait_ms from 8ms -> 4ms for small requests):
   - Result: fewer combined batches, p50 improved slightly; p95 unchanged. Increased per-request overhead, so throughput dropped ~4% in synthetic steady-state.

4) Kernel-level spin -> futex transition for batch assembly lock (Ethan):
   - Result: reduced tail latencies during very short stalls but increased latency variance. Appears to help when queue head contends under heavy interleaving of small and large requests.

Repro steps (how to trigger quickly):
- Use loadgen that mixes 80% small chitchat (<=32 tokens) at high qps + 20% long prompts (>=512 tokens) at low qps.
- Set KV store to use on-disk compressed values and set prefetch window to 6s.
- Run for 10 minutes and look at p50/95 traces; reproduce on single host with local loadgen.

Deep-dive notes (theory):
- Hypothesis A: Mixed-size batching causes repeated batch head churn. Small requests wait a few ms and then get coalesced with a large request; serialization path must allocate/move larger contiguous buffers resulting in stalls for subsequent small batches.
- Hypothesis B: Decompression on-hot-path occasionally runs concurrently with serialization leading to memory pressure and page thrashing.
- Hypothesis C: Our current batch metadata layout uses a single monolithic serialization buffer per batch; a spike of large-result items pushes small items into the same allocation, causing extra memcpy and GC pressure.

Metric snapshots (during spike):
- small_req_p50: 6.2ms (baseline 5.8ms)
- small_req_p95: 43.7ms (baseline 34.1ms)
- gpu_util: 72%
- host_cpu: 63% (was 53% in baseline)
- batch_size_mean: 4.6 -> spikes to 12 when long requests present

Potential fixes & tradeoffs (brainstorm):
- Option 1: Segmented serialization buffers (allocate per-item slices, then write iovec) — reduces big-copy but more complex kernel changes; lowers p95 but slightly higher allocations.
- Option 2: Prefer small-request micro-batches route (early-path fast lane) with fixed lower wait and small max batch cap — good for interactive UX but lowers aggregated throughput efficiency.
- Option 3: Eager decompression as background prefetch (kick off decompression earlier) to keep kernel path fast; requires more background job capacity and memory headroom.
- Option 4: Hybrid serialization format where small responses use a compact binary representation and large responses use chunked streaming (switch at 256 bytes).

Action items (who/what/when):
- Ethan: Prototype segmented serialization buffer (P0) — initial prototype by 2027-01-18. Aim: reduce memcpy count in serialize_batch() by 60%.
- Lina: Add metric for "decompression_on_serialize" (boolean) and a per-host counter for async_decompress_jobs; instrument by 2027-01-14.
- Rahul: Create a reproducible loadgen recipe (mix percentages + delay distributions) and add to RT-783 by 2027-01-13.
- Priya: Draft canary plan for small-request fast lane (safety rollback criteria, rollout %s) by 2027-01-15.

Open questions / discussion points for next sync:
- Is the complexity of segmented buffers worth kernel maintenance burden?
- How long can we tolerate extra memory footprint for eager decompression before it impacts host OOM risk?
- Do we prefer a graceful degradation (fast lane) vs systemic fix (segmented buffers)?

Notes to future readers / scratchpad:
- There were two hosts with kernel builds older than the canary; they did not show the anomaly. Investigate build diff.
- The tracing header we currently sample at 1% — consider bumping to 5% for the next canary to get better signal.
- Put a small telemetry gauge for batch_serialize_work_ms in the /metrics endpoint.

Quick links and references:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve-runtime/pull/1428 (experimental json/flatbuffers switch)
- Jira: RT-783 (loadgen + reproducible recipe)
- Slack: #serving-runtime thread (see linked artifact)

Closing:
- This doc is intentionally messy. The goal is to capture the set of partial experiments we ran and keep the next steps tight. We should decide at next Wednesday sync whether to move forward with segmented serialization prototype or the fast-lane canary.

-- Priya
